title: U.S. Backs Kenya’s Push to Process Critical Minerals Locally
desc: The U.S. says it will support Kenya’s critical-minerals sector, with local processing and value addition at the centre of the push.
content:
Kenya’s plans to develop its critical-minerals sector have received fresh backing from the United States, which says it is ready to support the country in building local processing capacity.

The development puts renewed focus on Kenya’s strategic mineral resources, including the Mrima Hill deposit in Kwale County, which is expected to contain rare earth minerals and niobium. The minerals are important for industries including aerospace and advanced manufacturing.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Africa Frank Garcia said Washington wants to work with Kenya to develop a mining sector that attracts legitimate investment, respects local communities and strengthens global supply chains.

President William Ruto welcomed the support, saying Kenya is accelerating the responsible exploration and development of rare earth elements and other strategic minerals. He also linked local processing and value addition to the creation of jobs and greater domestic economic benefits.

The Mrima Hill project is currently attracting interest from international companies. Six companies are understood to be in contention to develop the deposit, including two U.S.-based consortia, although Kenya has not publicly released an official shortlist.

The push comes as the United States seeks to strengthen alternative sources of critical minerals amid growing global competition over access to resources dominated by China.

For Kenya, the bigger issue is not simply extracting minerals from the ground. The U.S. has indicated that it supports a model in which more processing and value addition takes place in the countries where the minerals are found.

If successfully implemented, such an approach could create opportunities beyond mining itself, including jobs, investment, technical skills and new industrial activity.

However, the development of Mrima Hill remains subject to Kenya’s ongoing tender process, meaning the potential economic benefits have yet to materialise.

The fresh U.S. backing therefore adds another significant international dimension to Kenya’s efforts to position its mineral resources as a source of investment, employment and long-term economic growth.
